summary: Two ivory leaves, each divided into three scenes by acanthus borders, show six miracles of Christ: the Raising of Lazarus, the Wedding at Cana, the Healing of the Leper, the Multiplication of the Loaves and Fishes, the Healing of the Blind Man and the Healing of the Paralytic. In every panel a youthful, beardless Christ stretches out his hand or staff in a gesture of power, set against carefully drawn brick walls and buildings. The diptych is a fine witness to how the Carolingian court looked back to Early Christian art to picture the Lord as healer and giver of life.
facts: The V&A notes that its date is highly controversial: once taken for Late Antique work, it is now generally attributed to the Carolingian Renaissance of the 9th century, and the leaves may have been re-carved from a Late Antique diptych.
Faint painted figures of two haloed saints survive on the backs, and a large keyhole was cut into one leaf when the diptych was later reused, probably as the doors of a tabernacle or reliquary.
It was formerly at Palermo and in the Currie collection, and was given to the museum by F. E. Andrews through the National Art Collections Fund.

summary: This five-part ivory leaf, used as the cover of a gospel book, sets a bearded Christ enthroned beneath an arch at its centre, flanked by two standing apostles. Narrow side panels with standing figures and small narrative scenes surround him, and the lowest band shows the story of Jonah cast into the sea and swallowed by the great fish, the Old Testament sign of the Resurrection; above, two flying angels carry a wreath with a cross. The whole composition proclaims Christ as the enthroned Lord of the Church, framed by his deeds and by prophecy.
facts: It is known as the 'Murano Diptych' and is displayed in the ivory room of the Museo Nazionale in Ravenna; the museum's attribution, as recorded with the photographs, is 'perhaps Egyptian', about 500–550.
Five-part ivory covers of this kind, with a large central panel surrounded by four narrow panels, were a prestigious form of gospel-book binding in the 5th and 6th centuries (type).

links.label: Wikimedia Commons category (Ivory in the Museo nazionale, Ravenna)

notes: Only one leaf survives in Ravenna. Detailed identification of every small side scene could not be verified from an accessible museum record.

summary: Within a beaded roundel set in a frame of lush acanthus, Christ appears in half-length with a cross-nimbus, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a closed book against his chest. His calm, frontal face and the simple folds of his mantle give the small plaque the gravity of an icon. It belongs to the revival of Late Antique forms under Charlemagne, when ivory carvers again presented Christ as the teacher and Lord of the Gospel.
facts: The museum groups this plaque with a companion plaque showing the angel, symbol of St Matthew, both attributed to Carolingian North Italy around 790–810.
Such square plaques were typically set into the jewelled or carved covers of gospel books, where Christ was often surrounded by the evangelists' symbols (type).

links.label: Wikimedia Commons category (Ivory in the Museo nazionale, Ravenna)

summary: Under a pierced arch the central panel shows the Nativity: the Virgin reclines beside the manger where the swaddled Christ Child lies with the ox and ass, angels crowd above, Joseph sits pensively below and midwives bathe the newborn. The wings continue the story in small, densely carved scenes, among them the Entry into Jerusalem and the Ascension with Christ enthroned among angels. A portable devotional triptych of this kind gathered the great feasts of Christ's life into a single object for private prayer.
facts: The Louvre dates the triptych to 950–1000 on stylistic grounds and attributes it to Constantinople under the Macedonian dynasty.
It passed through the celebrated collections of Prince Alexis Soltykoff (sold 1861), Frédéric Spitzer and Edmond Foulc before the Louvre acquired it from Raoul Duseigneur in 1900.
notes: Original title: Triptyque : la Nativité.

summary: A round ivory box, cut from a section of elephant tusk, is carved around its wall with scenes of Christ's ministry, including his meeting with the Samaritan woman at the well and miracles of healing. In the late Middle Ages the pyxis was mounted on a slender copper foot and capped with a conical lid and cross, turning it into a vessel for church use. It shows how Early Christian images of Christ the life-giver continued to be treasured and reused for centuries.
facts: According to the Louvre, this pyxis and a second one of different workmanship lost their original ivory bases and lids and were made into a pair by a simple Gothic copper mount whose foot is engraved with the name 'IESUS' in Gothic letters.
The pyxides come from Lavoûte-Chilhac (Haute-Loire); they were classified as historic monuments in 1897 and acquired from the town's mayor in 1901.
notes: Original title: Pyxide de Lavoûte-Chilhac : le Christ et la Samaritaine ; Miracles du Christ.

summary: This crowded Ottonian plaque reads like a whole Easter sermon. At the centre Christ hangs on the cross beneath the titulus IHS NAZARENUS REX IUDEORUM, flanked by Sol and Luna, with a chalice at the foot of the cross; below, the Virgin and John stand on one side and the holy women approach the angel at the empty tomb on the other. Above, Christ is enthroned in a starry mandorla between Alpha and Omega, while at the upper right he ascends, grasping the hand of God as a crowd of apostles looks up.
facts: The plaque was made to decorate a book binding; it combines four moments, from the Crucifixion to the Second Coming, in a single vertical field.
The Ascension shown with Christ striding upward and taking the hand of God reaching from heaven is a characteristically Western, Carolingian–Ottonian formula (type).
notes: Original title: Plaque de reliure : crucifixion, saintes femmes au tombeau, ascension et Christ bénissant. Date and place follow the photographers' captions (Rhineland, late 10th–early 11th century); the museum record was not accessible.

summary: In the arched central panel Christ hangs on a tall cross, with angels and the sun and moon above and the Virgin and St John standing on either side; below, the emperor Constantine and his mother Helena flank the foot of the cross, recalling the finding of the True Cross. The wings carry columns of saints in medallions joined by a vine-like band. The triptych unites the saving death of Christ with the imperial veneration of the cross that was so central to Byzantine piety.
facts: The pairing of the Crucifixion with Constantine and Helena links Christ's sacrifice to the legend of Helena's discovery of the True Cross in Jerusalem (iconographic tradition).

The object is digitised on Gallica by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which describes it as an elephant-ivory triptych with the Crucifixion and saints, made in Constantinople in the second half of the 10th century.

summary: A half-length Christ fills this ivory plaque, his bearded face framed by long hair and a cross-nimbus, the abbreviation of his name carved on either side. He raises his right hand in blessing and holds against his chest a gospel book with a jewelled cover. The intense, frontal gaze is the image of the Pantocrator, the Ruler of All, that Byzantine artists placed in domes, on coins and on precious objects alike.
facts: The museum label identifies it as a Byzantine work of the late 10th or early 11th century, 12.9 cm high, inventory L 412.
The bust of Christ holding a book and blessing became, after the end of Iconoclasm in 843, the standard Byzantine image of Christ Pantocrator (type).

summary: Beneath a pierced canopy the Virgin sits on a cushioned throne, holding the Christ Child frontally on her lap, while two small busts in medallions look on from the upper corners. The Child sits upright like a little emperor, blessing, the Lord enthroned in the lap of his Mother. The tall, slender proportions and delicate openwork are typical of the finest ivories of 10th-century Constantinople.
facts: The plaque is attributed to Constantinople around 950–1000, the period sometimes called the 'Macedonian Renaissance' of Byzantine ivory carving.
The Virgin enthroned with the Child seated frontally on her knees (the Kyriotissa type) presents Mary as the throne of Christ (type).

summary: Christ hangs upon the cross with his head gently inclined, his body long and slender, wearing a loincloth; small angels and busts appear at the top beneath a canopy. To the left the Virgin raises her hand in grief, and to the right St John stands holding a book. This quiet, symmetrical composition is the classic Middle Byzantine image of the Crucifixion, inviting contemplation rather than drama.
facts: It is described as a plaque from a gospel-book cover, carved in Byzantium at the end of the 10th century.
The three-figure Crucifixion with the Virgin and John alone beside the cross was the most common Byzantine form of the scene in ivory (type).
notes: The Commons caption calls it a 'Deesis' plaque, but the image clearly shows the Crucifixion with the Virgin and St John.

summary: Beneath an arcade Christ rides sideways on a donkey toward the gate of Jerusalem, followed by his disciples, while the people come out to meet him, children spread garments in his path and a boy climbs a tree to cut branches. The scene is carved in deep relief with many small figures, yet Christ's calm, upright figure remains the clear focus. In the Byzantine cycle of feasts this image announced Palm Sunday and the beginning of the Passion.
facts: The panel was the centre of a triptych; its wings, now lost, would have folded over it to protect the image (type).
The Entry into Jerusalem was one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine Church, frequently represented on ivories and icons (type).

summary: Three horizontal registers tell three Gospel stories: at the top the boy Jesus sits among the teachers in the Temple, in the middle Christ changes water into wine at the wedding at Cana, and at the bottom he heals a leper. The many small figures move with a lively, rhythmic energy characteristic of Carolingian ivory carving at Metz. Read together, the scenes show Christ revealing his wisdom and his divine power at the beginning of his public life.
facts: Metz, the see of Charlemagne's son Drogo, was one of the leading centres of Carolingian ivory carving in the 9th century.
Plaques arranged in narrative registers like this one were usually set into book covers (type).

summary: Christ bends low over a basin to wash the feet of Peter, who sits at the head of the gathered apostles and raises his hand in protest. The other disciples crowd behind on a bench, watching, beneath a draped canopy; a Greek inscription names the scene. The image captures the humility of the Lord who 'came not to be served but to serve', a key moment in the Byzantine Passion cycle.
facts: In Byzantine art the Washing of the Feet is shown with Peter touching his head or raising his hand, recalling his words 'Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head' (iconographic tradition).
Small ivory icons of single feasts like this one were produced in Constantinople in the 10th century for private devotion (type).

summary: Christ, followed by his apostles, strides toward the tomb and stretches out his right hand, commanding Lazarus to come forth; Lazarus stands wrapped in his grave-bands in an arched tomb while a servant unwinds them. Martha and Mary kneel at Christ's feet in gratitude. Coming just before Palm Sunday in the Byzantine calendar, the Raising of Lazarus was celebrated as a pledge of the general resurrection.
facts: In the Byzantine Church the Saturday before Palm Sunday is still called 'Lazarus Saturday', and this scene was one of the regular feast images (tradition).
Traces of gilding on the figures show that such ivories were originally enriched with colour and gold (type).

summary: Christ hangs on the cross beneath a starry sky with two mourning angels, the Virgin standing at the left and St John at the right. At the foot of the cross a small figure kneels in prostration, the donor who commissioned the relief, placing himself literally beneath the saving cross. The image joins the universal mystery of Calvary with one person's plea for mercy.
facts: Donor portraits in proskynesis (full prostration) at the foot of the cross or before Christ are a recurring feature of Middle Byzantine devotional objects (type).

summary: Under a pierced canopy Christ stands frontally on a footstool, holding a book and blessing, while the Virgin Mary and St John the Baptist turn toward him with hands raised in supplication. This group, the Deesis ('entreaty'), shows the two greatest saints interceding with Christ for humanity. Its quiet symmetry made it one of the most beloved Byzantine images of prayer.
facts: The Deesis became a central Byzantine theme from the 10th century, appearing on ivories, icons and later on the templon screens of churches (type).

summary: Christ is crucified high in the upper part of the panel, with mourning angels above the cross. Below, the Virgin and the holy women stand at the left, while at the right a group of helmeted soldiers gathers. The fuller, more narrative version of Calvary contrasts the sorrow of the faithful with the indifference of the executioners.
facts: Byzantine ivory carvers produced both the simple three-figure Crucifixion and fuller narrative versions with soldiers and mourners, sometimes in the same workshop (type).

summary: Within an arched frame whose columns and canopy still carry much of their gilding, Christ hangs on the cross with a golden halo, flanked by the Virgin and St John, with angels in the upper corners. The well-preserved gold gives a rare idea of how luminous these ivories originally appeared. The serene body of Christ, alive in death, expresses the Byzantine understanding of the Crucifixion as victory.
facts: Gilding and paint once covered parts of many Byzantine ivories; this relief preserves unusually extensive traces of it (type).

summary: On the left leaf Moses reaches up to receive the tablets of the Law from the hand of God; on the right the risen Christ, standing in a doorway, lifts his arm to reveal the wound in his side as Thomas reaches out to touch it. The two tall, slender figures in rich architectural frames set the Old Covenant beside the New. Christ's gesture offers the doubting apostle — and every viewer — tangible proof of the Resurrection.
facts: The Bode-Museum acquired the two leaves in 1935 (inv. nos. 8505/8506); they are attributed to Trier at the end of the 10th century, when Archbishop Egbert made the city a leading artistic centre.
Pairing Moses receiving the Law with Thomas touching Christ's wound sets the giving of the Old Law beside the revelation of the risen Lord (typological reading).

summary: Christ sits enthroned in a mandorla at the centre of the plaque, raising his hand in blessing, beneath a draped curtain. Around him the four evangelists sit writing at their desks, each inspired by his symbol, so that the Gospels seem to flow from the Lord in majesty. The composition presents Christ as the living Word proclaimed by the four Gospels.
facts: According to the photographer's documentation the plaque was donated to the Berlin museum by J. Werner in 1898 (inv. 2423).
Christ in Majesty surrounded by the evangelists was a favourite subject for the front covers of Ottonian gospel books (type).

summary: The Virgin lies on her bier surrounded by the grieving apostles, Peter at her head and Paul bowing at her feet. Behind the bier Christ stands in a mandorla-like space, holding in his arms his Mother's soul in the form of a small swaddled child, while angels descend from above to carry it to heaven. The scene beautifully reverses the Nativity: the Son now cradles his Mother as she once cradled him.
facts: The Dormition (Koimesis) is not narrated in the New Testament but in later apocryphal accounts; it became one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine Church, celebrated on 15 August (tradition).
Ivory plaques of the Koimesis were especially numerous in 10th-century Constantinople, and several were later set into Western book covers (type).

summary: The Virgin lies in death on a draped bier while the apostles crowd around in mourning. At the centre, behind the bier, Christ stands looking down, holding his Mother's soul as a small swaddled figure; two angels swoop down from above with veiled hands to receive it. Carved in deep, crisp relief, the plaque expresses the Byzantine faith that death for Christ's Mother was a falling asleep into his arms.
facts: Byzantine ivories of the Dormition reached the West early; Ottonian patrons valued them highly and often reused them on book covers (type).

summary: Christ stands on a low footstool in the centre, identified by the letters IC XC, holding a book and blessing; on either side the Virgin and St John the Baptist, both named by inscriptions, incline toward him with hands raised in prayer. The three tall figures are carved almost in the round against a plain ground. The Deesis expresses the intercession of the saints before the Lord who is both judge and saviour.
facts: The Deesis group — Christ between the Virgin and the Baptist — was a frequent subject of Middle Byzantine ivories and later formed the core of the iconostasis (type).

summary: Beneath an arch, Christ hangs on the cross with a large halo, his head bowed and his long body gently swaying; the Virgin raises her hand in grief at the left, while St John stands at the right, his hand to his cheek. The restrained composition gives the Crucifixion the stillness of an icon.
facts: Byzantine crucifixion ivories of the later 10th century often show Christ's body in a gentle curve with the head inclined in death, a type that spread to the West (type).

summary: The Virgin is shown in half-length holding the Christ Child on her left arm and pointing to him with her right hand, while two small busts of angels or saints appear in the upper corners. The Child, robed like an adult, sits upright and blesses. This is the Hodegetria ('She who shows the way'), in which Mary directs the viewer to her Son as the way to salvation.
facts: The Hodegetria type was named after a famous icon kept in the Hodegon monastery in Constantinople (tradition).
The Freising museum label describes the plaque as Byzantine, around 1000.

summary: This small round medallion shows Christ in bust, with full curling hair and a short beard, clothed in a mantle and holding a book. Although worn, the face keeps a youthful, gentle expression typical of the 6th century. Medallions of this kind were set into larger objects, such as book covers or caskets, where the image of Christ crowned the composition.
facts: The museum catalogues it as BXM 835 and dates it to the 6th century.
A similar medallion bust of Christ held by angels crowns the upper panel of the Barberini Ivory in the Louvre, showing how such images were used (comparison).

summary: Christ sits on a high-backed throne with a bolster cushion, his feet on a footstool, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a book on his knee. Plant scrolls fill the background on either side of the throne. Carved not from elephant ivory but from whale bone, the plaque shows how the image of Christ in majesty was reproduced in more modest materials.
facts: Whale bone and walrus ivory were used as substitutes when elephant ivory was scarce, particularly in the West in the 10th and 11th centuries (type).
notes: Place of production is uncertain; the museum caption gives only 'mid-10th century, whale bone'.

summary: This wooden casket is clad with ivory plaques showing busts of Christ, the Virgin and saints in arched frames, separated by bands of rosettes. Arranged like the figures of a templon screen, the holy persons turn the box into a small reliquary or treasure chest guarded by Christ and his saints. Byzantine workshops produced both secular rosette caskets and religious ones like this.
facts: 'Rosette caskets' with borders of carved rosettes were made in Constantinople mainly in the 10th and 11th centuries; most show mythological subjects, making religious examples rarer (type).

summary: At the top, Christ sits in a round glory borne aloft by two angels with outspread wings; below, between two stylised trees and beneath a Greek inscription, and the twelve apostles with the Virgin stand gazing upward. The clear division between heaven above and earth below expresses the meaning of the feast: the Lord who ascends will return in glory.
facts: The panel was the centre of a triptych, whose hinged wings would have closed over it (type).

The Ascension, celebrated forty days after Easter, was one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine Church and is often shown, as here, with the Virgin standing among the apostles (iconographic tradition).

summary: In the central panel Christ sits on a richly carved throne with bolster cushions, blessing, while the Virgin and St John the Baptist stand at either side in supplication; further saints stand on the wings in rows. The serene, classically draped figures belong to the most refined group of Constantinopolitan ivories. The triptych places the viewer before the heavenly court, with Christ enthroned as Judge and Saviour.
facts: The Deesis — Christ between the interceding Virgin and John the Baptist — is the central theme of several of the finest 10th-century Constantinopolitan ivory triptychs, among them the Harbaville Triptych in the Louvre (comparison).

summary: Christ, standing on a footstool and identified by the letters IC XC, lays his hand upon the crown of the emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, who bows slightly before him in jewelled imperial dress. Inscriptions name the emperor as autokrator. The plaque makes visible the Byzantine conviction that the emperor's authority came directly from Christ.
facts: The plaque is usually dated around 945, when Constantine VII became sole emperor after the deposition of the Lekapenos family.
It belongs to a small group of imperial ivories, together with the Romanos Ivory in Paris, showing Christ crowning the ruler (comparison).

summary: Carved fully in the round, the slender Mother of God stands holding the Christ Child on her left arm and gestures toward him with her right hand, showing him as the Way. The Child sits upright, holding a scroll and blessing. Almost unique as a freestanding Byzantine statuette, it preserves the form of the venerated Hodegetria icon in three dimensions.
facts: The V&A describes it as the sole surviving example of freestanding Byzantine ivory sculpture; it was probably placed in a small tabernacle so that it could be seen from all sides.

The head of the Christ Child is a 19th-century restoration, most probably made in the Castellani workshop in Rome; a lozenge pattern of dots on the Virgin's cloak suggests it was once painted and gilded.
It was bought from the collection of Alessandro Castellani in Rome in 1884.

summary: Beneath a pierced arcade Christ stands frontally on a footstool, holding a book and blessing; the Virgin at the left and St John the Baptist at the right lift their hands toward him in intercession. The tall, finely draped figures stand in a shallow space, isolated against the plain ivory ground. The plaque is a compact image of the Church's prayer before Christ.
facts: The British Museum dates the plaque to about 900–1000 (registration number 1923,1205.2) and displays it in Room 40.

summary: John the Baptist, bearded and wearing a rough garment, lays his hand on the head of the young, naked Christ, who stands in the waters of the Jordan; the dove of the Holy Spirit descends from above, and angels attend with cloths. A small reclining figure at the bottom represents the river Jordan itself, a survival of classical personification. The panel shows the moment when Christ was revealed as the beloved Son.
facts: Early Christian images of the Baptism often show Christ as a small, youthful, naked figure and include a personification of the river Jordan, as here (type).

summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a throne holding the Christ Child on her lap, while the three Magi in Persian caps approach from either side bearing gifts and an angel stands behind. In a band beneath, the Nativity is shown with the Child in the manger. The solemn, hieratic arrangement presents the Child as King, receiving the homage of the nations.
facts: Commons classifies the panel as a 6th-century Byzantine ivory displayed in Room 41 of the British Museum.
Showing the Magi approaching a frontally enthroned Virgin and Child, rather than in profile, was an Eastern innovation of the 6th century (type).

summary: Christ strides forward with an apostle behind him, his hand extended toward the tomb, where Lazarus stands upright in his grave-clothes inside an arched niche; one of the sisters kneels at Christ's feet. Buildings of the town of Bethany rise in the background. The slim panel captures the instant of Christ's command, 'Lazarus, come forth'.
facts: The British Museum catalogues the plaque as Byzantine Empire or Italy (Venice?), about 900–1000, showing that the attribution of such ivories between Byzantium and its Italian imitators can be difficult.

summary: At the right, Christ appears in a great circular glory, enthroned on a footstool and holding an inscribed tablet, with a host of angels behind him. At the left a haloed figure, identified as the prophet Ezekiel, stands before a city wall and stretches out his hand, while small figures rise from the ground below — the dry bones coming to life. The panel links Ezekiel's vision of the resurrection of the dead with Christ's victory over death.
facts: The British Museum describes the subject as 'the Descent of Our Lord into Hell (Anastasis; Vision of Ezekiel)' and dates the panel to about 900–1000.
notes: The precise subject is debated; the museum title combines the Anastasis and the Vision of Ezekiel. Christ's presence in the glory is clear, but the reading of the left-hand figure follows the museum's interpretation.

summary: Christ hangs on the cross between the sun and moon, his body slightly swaying, with the Virgin standing at the left and St John at the right holding a book. The figures are carved with broad, simple forms and stand on a narrow ground line beneath the cross. The plaque belongs to a group of ivories whose sober, monumental style is associated with the reign of Nikephoros II Phokas.
facts: The museum attributes it to the 'Nikephoros Group', a set of ivories named after the ivory staurotheke (cross reliquary) at Cortona, which bears the name of the emperor Nikephoros II Phokas (963–969).

summary: Within a frame of carved ornament the Virgin lies on her bier, mourned by the apostles who bend toward her from both sides. Behind the bier stands Christ, holding the little swaddled figure of her soul, while angels fly in from the upper corners. The horizontal format allows the mourners to unfold in a quiet, rhythmic procession around the central figure of the Lord.
facts: In the Koimesis, Christ receiving his Mother's soul is the visual centre of the composition; the image became one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine year (tradition).

summary: Under an arched canopy Christ hangs on the cross, his head bowed and his body in a gentle curve, between the grieving Virgin and St John. Busts of angels appear in the upper corners and a small mound marks Golgotha at the foot of the cross. The warm tone of the ivory and the deep cutting give the figures a strong, almost sculptural presence.
facts: Leaves of this kind were once hinged to a companion panel, often showing the Virgin or another feast, to form a small folding icon (type).

summary: A tall, frontal Christ, flanked by two angels, carries a cross over his shoulder and a book, and stands upon a lion and a serpent-like dragon. A Latin inscription runs across the top of the frame, and the surrounding border is filled with interlace and inlaid blue glass. The plaque illustrates Psalm 91, read as a prophecy of Christ trampling the powers of evil; its companion leaf shows the Annunciation and the Visitation.
facts: Wikipedia's article on the theme lists it among the few works showing Christ treading on the beasts, describing it as 'either a much more provincial version of Carolingian style, or Northumbrian', with four beasts.
The museum label attributes the two plaques, found at Genoels-Elderen in Belgium, perhaps to the Rhine–Meuse region in the late 8th century.

links.label: Wikipedia: Christ treading on the beasts

notes: Wikipedia speaks of four beasts; in the photograph a lion and a dragon/serpent are clearly visible beneath Christ's feet.

summary: Five ivory panels form one of the grandest Carolingian book covers: at the top two angels hold a medallion with the bust of Christ blessing; in the centre the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child, between St John the Baptist and the prophet Zacharias; and at the bottom are the Nativity and the Annunciation to the Shepherds. Classical architecture and drapery show how deliberately Charlemagne's artists revived the art of Late Antiquity. The cover proclaims the Incarnation: the eternal Son, blessing from heaven, born of the Virgin.
facts: The V&A explains that the panels formed the front cover of the Lorsch Gospels, a Gospel book of about 810 listed in the Lorsch abbey library catalogue of about 860; the back cover, with Christ treading on the beasts, is in the Museo Sacro of the Vatican.
The manuscript was taken to Heidelberg in 1556 with the Bibliotheca Palatina and divided; its first volume is now in Alba Iulia (Batthyaneum) and the second in the Vatican.
In 2023 UNESCO inscribed the whole group of ivories and manuscripts in its Memory of the World register.
notes: Companion of the existing featured entry 'lorsch-gospels-ivory-christ-treading-beasts' (Vatican back cover); this is a separate object.

summary: Two leaves, each with three arcaded fields, present the four evangelists writing beneath their symbols, then the Nativity — the Child lying in the manger with ox and ass beside the Virgin and Joseph — and the Annunciation, and finally the angel greeting the holy women at the tomb and the Crucifixion. On the cross Christ stands upright and alive between Mary and John, with the lance-bearer and sponge-bearer below and the sun and moon above. The diptych gathers the beginning and the saving end of Christ's earthly life under the witness of the Gospels.
facts: The museum label attributes the diptych to the Court School of Charlemagne around 800, the same milieu that produced the ivory covers of the Lorsch Gospels.
Its six fields combine the four evangelists with four Gospel scenes, so that the writers of the Gospels literally stand above the events they recorded.

summary: This ivory holy-water bucket is carved in two rows with twelve scenes of Christ's Passion and Resurrection, from the Washing of the Feet and the Betrayal through the Crucifixion to the Harrowing of Hell, Christ's appearances to the women and the apostles, and the Incredulity of Thomas. Small, expressive figures move beneath arcades, while bands of inscription run around the rim. Holy water sprinkled from it over the faithful would have been linked visually to Christ's saving death and rising.
facts: The V&A believes it was made around 980 for the visit of Emperor Otto II, with Theophanu and the infant Otto III, to Milan; only three Ottonian ivory situlae survive (Milan c. 979, this one, and Aachen c. 1000).
Two of its three inscribed bands quote the Carmen Paschale of Sedulius, a 5th-century verse retelling of the Bible.
It passed through the Spitzer and Basilewsky collections and belonged to Tsar Alexander III and the Hermitage before coming to the V&A in 1933.

summary: At the centre of a field of gold reliefs, gems and enamels is an ivory plaque of the Crucifixion by an Echternach master: Christ hangs heavily on the cross, flanked by the lance-bearer and the sponge-bearer, with a figure of Earth beneath his feet. The surrounding gold panels show the rivers of Paradise with the evangelist symbols, saints and the imperial donors. The cover, older than the manuscript it now protects, makes the Cross the centre of the Gospel book and of the whole created world.
facts: German Wikipedia notes that the cover was probably made between 985 and 991 in Trier, in workshops working for Archbishop Egbert, as a gift of Empress Theophanu and her son Otto III, who appear as donors among the gold reliefs; it was joined to the Echternach gospel pages soon after 1031.
The gold reliefs around the ivory show the four rivers of Paradise with the evangelist symbols, the Virgin, St Peter, St Willibrord, St Benedict, St Boniface and St Liudger.

summary: In the centre of this jewelled gold cover Christ sits enthroned in majesty in a mandorla, holding the book of life and blessing. Around him, embossed gold reliefs show the four evangelists and scenes from his ministry, all framed by a dense setting of sapphires, emeralds and pearls. One of the very few surviving Carolingian treasure bindings, it gives the Gospels a cover worthy of the King it proclaims.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the cover can be precisely dated to 870 and was made for Emperor Charles the Bald in his Palace School, whose location may then have been the abbey of Saint-Denis.
Charles the Bald gave the book to Arnulf of Carinthia, who donated it to St Emmeram's Abbey in Regensburg, from which it takes its name.
The upper cover of the Lindau Gospels and the Arnulf Ciborium are attributed to the same workshop.

links.label: Wikipedia: Codex Aureus of St. Emmeram

summary: Christ hangs on a jewelled cross at the centre of this golden cover, his body straight and serene, his eyes open, with no sign of suffering. Small mourning figures and angels in gold repoussé surround the cross, and great raised clusters of gems fill the four fields between its arms. Here the Crucifixion is presented as triumph, the cross transformed into a throne of glory.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the upper cover is late Carolingian work of about 880, while the older lower cover is Insular-style work of the later 8th century, probably made in present-day Austria.
When J. P. Morgan bought the book in 1901 it was his first major purchase of a medieval manuscript; it still bears the shelfmark M.1.

summary: The ivory tablet on the front cover of this gospel lectionary shows Christ seated in majesty within a mandorla, raising his hand in blessing, surrounded by the symbols of the evangelists and by angels, framed above and below by dense panels of vine-scroll. The cover is set in a frame of gems. It is the masterwork associated with the St Gall monk Tuotilo and one of the treasures of the abbey library.
facts: Tuotilo (died 915) was a monk of St Gall praised by Ekkehard IV a century later as poet, musician, painter and sculptor; Wikipedia notes that works in media other than music are attributed to him with less certainty.
The manuscript, called the 'Evangelium longum' for its tall format, is fully digitised on e-codices.
notes: The date (c. 894) follows the Commons/e-codices metadata for the manuscript; the attribution of the carving to Tuotilo is traditional.

summary: In the upper part of this ivory plaque Christ sits in majesty in a mandorla, blessing, surrounded by the four evangelist symbols; below, Bishop Notger of Liège kneels in prayer before a small church building. The plaque, framed by later Mosan enamels and gilded lobes, covers a gospel book that belonged to the collegiate church of St John the Evangelist in Liège. It is a moving image of a bishop entrusting himself and his foundation to Christ.
facts: According to the Grand Curtius label, the gospel book belonged until the early 18th century to the collegiate church of Saint-Jean-l'Évangéliste in Liège, founded by Bishop Notger; the manuscript itself was written and illuminated at Reims around 930.

Notker (Notger) was bishop of Liège from 972 to 1008 and the city's first prince-bishop; Wikipedia notes that he founded St John's on the model of Aachen and appears to have commissioned this Evangeliary.

summary: Christ, followed by apostles, raises his hand toward a possessed man, while a small winged demon flees from the man's head and swine rush away at the lower right. The scene is set against a characteristic chequered openwork background, through which a gold ground once shone. It belongs to the series of small plaques that once decorated an altar or pulpit given by Otto I to his new cathedral at Magdeburg.
facts: Wikipedia notes that 16 Magdeburg Ivories survive; they were commissioned by Otto I, probably for the dedication of Magdeburg Cathedral and the raising of the see to an archbishopric in 968, for an object variously conjectured to be an antependium, throne, door or pulpit.
They are often assumed to have been made in Milan, though Peter Lasko argued for artists trained in Lorraine; the openwork backgrounds probably revealed a gilded backing.

summary: Beneath a tiled roof the apostles stand behind a low wall in three arches; in the left-hand arch the haloed, risen Christ raises his right arm while Thomas bends forward to touch the wound in his side. In the centre a firmly bolted door recalls that Christ came to the disciples 'when the doors were shut'. The architectural setting turns the Gospel episode into a vivid image of the risen Lord present among his Church.
facts: It is one of the 16 surviving Magdeburg Ivories commissioned by Otto I, each measuring nearly 13 by 12 cm (Wikipedia).

summary: Two moments of the Passion share this openwork plaque: at the left Christ is bound to a column and scourged by soldiers, while at the right Pilate, seated beneath a curtain, washes his hands as a servant pours water. Christ, taller than his tormentors and haloed, remains calm and upright. The pierced plant and architectural background is typical of the Magdeburg series.
facts: The Magdeburg Ivories show an unusual emphasis on Christ's ministry, and two further panels are known only from 16th-century drawings (Wikipedia).
The photographer's caption identifies this plaque as one of the reliefs donated to Magdeburg Cathedral by Otto I, made in Milan between 962 and 973.
notes: Image is small (468 px).

summary: Around this ivory holy-water bucket runs a series of arches: in one the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child, between two angels, and the others hold the four evangelists writing their Gospels. A dedicatory inscription bands the rim. Made for an imperial ceremony, the situla places the Incarnate Word at the centre of the Gospel witness.
facts: The museum caption states that it was commissioned by Gotofredo, archbishop of Milan and protégé of Otto II, dedicated to the emperor and used in imperial ceremonies.
The V&A cites this 'Milan situla of about 979' as one of only three Ottonian ivory situlae to survive, with the Basilewsky Situla and one in Aachen.

summary: Christ sits enthroned between St Mary and St Maurice, raising his hands over a small imperial family who prostrate themselves at his feet: the emperor, the empress and a little crowned son. The inscription OTTO IMPERATOR runs along the base, and the letters IHS XPS name Christ above. The plaque expresses the Ottonian ideal of the emperor as the humble servant and representative of Christ the true King.
facts: The V&A notes that this relief of Christ enthroned with the Emperor Otto II, his wife and child is stylistically related to the Basilewsky Situla, suggesting both were made in Milan around 980.
The figures are usually identified as Otto II, Theophanu and the infant Otto III, though some have proposed Otto I and Adelaide.
notes: The flanking saints are identified by the inscriptions SCA MARIA and SCS MAURICIUS visible on the frame. Image is small (486 px).

summary: On the left leaf of this book cover Christ sits in majesty on a footstool, holding a book and blessing, while the twelve apostles are seated around him in tiers, turning toward him in discussion. The right leaf carries openwork scrolls with medallions of the evangelist symbols. The composition presents Christ as Teacher among the apostolic college, the source of the Gospel the book contains.
facts: The museum dates the cover to the 10th century; the lattice and scroll frames are carved in openwork so that the wood or a coloured ground would show through (type).

summary: At the top of this tall plaque Christ ascends in a mandorla toward the hand of God that reaches down from the clouds, flanked by angels. Beneath, the apostles look up in amazement around a central haloed figure with raised arms, and in the lowest register a crowd gathers before a gabled building within city walls. The swirling, agitated figures are typical of the Liuthard Group, the ivory carvers of Charles the Bald's court.
facts: The museum label attributes the cover to the Liuthard Group, named after the scribe Liuthard who worked for Charles the Bald, in the second half of the 9th century.
notes: The subject of the lowest register could not be identified with confidence from the photograph.

summary: Within borders of inhabited vine scroll, the ivory shows Christ ascending in a mandorla, lifted by two angels toward the hand of God, while two further angels bow beneath and the Virgin and the apostles gather below, gazing upward. The ivory was later set in a silver-gilt frame. It belongs to the refined Metz school of Carolingian ivory carving.
facts: The Coburg collections describe it as the book cover of the Gandersheim Gospels, Metz ivory of about 860–870, with a silver-gilt frame added in 1555 (inv. Pl.001).

summary: On the left leaf Christ hangs on the cross beneath an inscription naming him, with the sun and moon above and the Virgin and St John at either side; below, the she-wolf suckles Romulus and Remus. The right leaf shows the Virgin enthroned in majesty with angels and, below, three saints. The diptych juxtaposes the saving death of Christ with a symbol of Rome, in a vigorous, unclassical style.
facts: Its traditional name links it to the abbey of Rambona in the Marche (central Italy), whose foundation it is believed to commemorate; the Vatican Museums display it in the Christian Museum.
The she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus beneath the cross is a rare appearance of this Roman emblem in a Christian ivory, usually read as a sign of Rome's place in salvation history.
notes: The connection with the abbey's foundation rests on the ivory's inscription as reported in the literature; the full inscription text could not be verified from an accessible source.

summary: In the centre Christ stands triumphant, carrying a cross over his shoulder and a book, trampling the lion, dragon, asp and basilisk. Twelve small surrounding panels narrate episodes from the Gospels, beginning with the Annunciation and Nativity and including miracles of Christ. The composition proclaims the victorious Lord whose earthly life, told around the edges, accomplished the defeat of evil.
facts: Wikipedia's article on Christ treading on the beasts calls it the 'Oxford book cover' and notes its four beasts, the full set named in the Vulgate verse.
The book it covers is MS Douce 176, measuring about 21 × 12 cm.

links.label: Wikipedia: Christ treading on the beasts

notes: Image is a black-and-white photograph.

summary: The jewelled front of this processional cross bears a cameo of Augustus, but its plain silver-gilt reverse is engraved with the crucified Christ, his head sinking in death, with the hand of God holding a wreath above and the dove of the Holy Spirit, and medallions at the ends of the arms. The contrast is deliberate: the triumphant imperial jewels on one side, the suffering Saviour on the other. Wikipedia notes that this engraving looks forward to Romanesque art.
facts: The cross takes its name from a rock-crystal seal of the Carolingian king Lothair II set near its base, although it was made over a century after his death, possibly for Otto III.
It is still carried in procession on high feast days and placed beside the main altar of Aachen Cathedral during Mass.
notes: Only the reverse depicts Christ; the engraving is faint at small sizes. Description of the medallions follows standard accounts.

summary: A golden processional cross set with gems and pearls carries a relief figure of the crucified Christ, and below his feet a cloisonné enamel plaque shows the two donors, Abbess Mathilde and her brother Duke Otto, holding the cross between them. The jewels honour the cross as the Tree of Life and the throne of the risen Lord. It is the oldest of the great Ottonian processional crosses in Essen.
facts: It is named after Otto I, Duke of Swabia and Bavaria, and his sister Mathilde, abbess of Essen, grandchildren of Emperor Otto I; since Mathilde became abbess in 973 and Otto died in 982 it is dated between these years.
The cross is 44.5 cm high, with an oak core, and was carried on high holidays until recently.

links.label: Wikipedia: Cross of Otto and Mathilde

summary: The gilt-bronze body of the crucified Christ hangs at the centre of this jewelled processional cross, his arms outstretched across a field of gold, gems and pearls. On the stem a small enamel shows Abbess Mathilde as donor, kneeling before the Virgin and Child. The crucifix itself contains cavities for relics, making the image of Christ also a reliquary.
facts: Wikipedia notes that it was made between about 1000 and 1058, perhaps in stages, and that the corpus may be a later replacement; the reverse bears a punched Agnus Dei with the evangelist symbols.
It forms a group with the Cross of Otto and Mathilde, the Senkschmelz Cross and the Cross of Theophanu, all made for Essen Abbey.
notes: Dating straddles the year 1000; included because it was begun under Mathilde (d. 1011).

summary: Instead of a sculpted corpus, this jewelled cross carries five large enamel plaques; the central one shows the Crucifixion, with Christ on the cross between the Virgin and St John, while the enamels at the ends of the arms show the evangelist symbols. The intense blues, greens and whites of the enamel glow amid the gold and gems. It is counted among the masterpieces of Ottonian goldsmiths' work.
facts: Its name refers to its five unusually large plaques of senkschmelz ('sunk') enamel, in which the enamel sits in recesses surrounded by plain gold; the border also held 24 small enamels, 21 of which survive.
Its block-shaped arm ends resemble the cubic capitals popular in architecture around the year 1000.

links.label: Wikipedia: Essen cross with large enamels

summary: The Virgin sits upright on a throne, holding a golden orb, while the Christ Child sits on her lap holding a book, both figures covered with thin sheets of beaten gold. Their large enamel eyes give the statue an arresting, living gaze. It is the oldest surviving sculpture of the Madonna and Child north of the Alps, and still a focus of prayer in Essen.
facts: Wikipedia notes that, dated around 980, it is both the oldest known sculpture of the Madonna and the oldest free-standing medieval sculpture north of the Alps; it is 74 cm high.
It was made during the tenure of Abbess Mathilde, granddaughter of Otto I; in 1959 Pope John XXIII named the image Our Lady of Good Counsel and patroness of the Diocese of Essen.

summary: The sliding lid of this reliquary for the True Cross is covered with nine enamel panels: at the centre Christ sits enthroned, flanked by the Virgin and St John the Baptist, with archangels and the twelve apostles arranged around them, the whole framed by gems and an inscription. Inside, a double-armed cross holds fragments of the True Cross. The Staurotheke is one of the finest surviving works of Byzantine cloisonné enamel.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the cross inside bears an inscription naming the emperors Constantine VII and Romanos II, who ruled jointly from 945 to 959; the box was made later.
It was probably brought to Germany as loot from the Fourth Crusade (1204); it measures 48 by 38 cm.
notes: The date of the box (c. 964–965, under Basil the Proedros) follows the standard literature; Wikipedia only states it was made after the cross.

summary: At the centre of the golden front of the high altar Christ is enthroned in a cross-shaped frame, surrounded by the symbols of the evangelists and the twelve apostles; panels on either side narrate the life of Christ, from the Annunciation and Nativity to miracles, the Crucifixion, Resurrection and Ascension. Gems and enamels set into filigree frames make the altar a shining reliquary-like casing. It is one of the supreme achievements of Carolingian goldsmiths' work, still in use over the relics of St Ambrose.
facts: Italian Wikipedia notes that it was made between 824 and 859 for Bishop Angilbert II and is signed by 'Vuolvino magister phaber' (Wolvinius), hence also called the Altar of Volvinio.
It stands over the relics of Saints Gervasius, Protasius and Ambrose, which can still be seen through a small window from the crypt.

summary: This monumental wooden figure of the crucified Christ hangs with arms stretched straight out, his body upright, head slightly bowed, wearing a long loincloth. The calm, dignified figure shows a Christ who reigns from the cross even in death. Together with the Gero Cross in Cologne it is one of the earliest large-scale crucifixes of the Middle Ages.
facts: German Wikipedia records that Bishop Bernward of Hildesheim gave the monumental crucifix to the convent of Ringelheim, where his sister Judith was abbess around 1000, possibly on the occasion of her death.
notes: Material details beyond 'wood' are not verified. The photo shows the crucifix as displayed in the Hildesheim Dommuseum (2019).

summary: Christ fills the centre of this gilt-bronze plaque, robed in a garment covered with spirals and interlace, his large head with wide-open eyes showing that he is alive upon the cross. Above his arms hover two angels, and below stand the lance-bearer and the sponge-bearer. Abstract Celtic ornament transforms the Crucifixion into a solemn, timeless image of Christ's victory.
facts: Wikipedia describes it as the earliest and largest (21 cm) of the eight surviving early medieval Irish crucifixion plaques, found in the 19th century in the churchyard of St John's near Rinnegan, Co. Roscommon.
Rivet holes show that it was originally attached to a larger wooden object such as a processional cross, book shrine or altarpiece.

summary: On the obverse a majestic, bearded Christ with long hair looks straight out, raising his right hand in blessing and holding the Gospels, with a cross behind his head; the legend calls him IhS CRISTOS REX REGNANTIUM, 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. On the reverse the emperor stands holding a cross on steps, styled 'servant of Christ'. With this issue the image of Christ appeared for the first time on a coin, carrying the face of the Lord into the hands of everyone in the empire.
facts: Wikipedia notes that Justinian II was the first emperor to include the image of Christ on coinage issued in his name, moving the emperor's portrait to the reverse.

According to Wikipedia's article on Byzantine coinage, this innovation prompted the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik to abandon figural imitations of Byzantine coins and create a purely epigraphic Islamic coinage.

The obverse legend names Christ 'Rex regnantium' and the reverse styles Justinian 'servus Christi', servant of Christ, expressing the emperor's subordination to the heavenly King (legend as recorded for this specimen).
notes: The second-reign type, with a different, curly-haired Christ, is already in the collection (Cleveland Museum of Art 2012.47; featured key 'solidus-of-justinian-ii-christ').

summary: The obverse shows the nimbate bust of Christ Pantokrator, raising his hand in blessing and holding the Gospels; the reverse shows the young emperor Michael III beside his mother, the regent Theodora, both crowned. Struck in the years after the end of Iconoclasm in 843, the coin announced across the empire that the image of Christ had been restored. The face of Christ returned to the coinage after an absence of nearly a century and a half.
facts: Wikipedia's article on Byzantine coinage notes that the type of Justinian II, with Christ on the obverse, was revived after the end of Iconoclasm and remained the norm until the end of the Empire.
Wikipedia notes that Theodora, as regent for Michael III, restored the veneration of icons in March 843, ending the second Byzantine Iconoclasm; she is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church.

summary: The obverse bears the bust of Christ Pantokrator with a cross behind his head, surrounded by the legend IhSUS XRISTOS, 'Jesus Christ'. On the reverse Michael III appears alone, crowned and holding a labarum. After his mother's removal from power the emperor kept Christ's image in the place of honour on the coinage.
facts: After the post-iconoclast revival, the bust of Christ on the obverse with the emperor on the reverse became the standard design of Byzantine gold coinage (Wikipedia, Byzantine coinage).

summary: Christ sits frontally on a lyre-backed throne, blessing and holding the Gospels, encircled by the legend IHS XPS REX REGNANTIUM, 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. On the reverse Leo VI and his young son Constantine VII stand together holding a patriarchal cross. Christ enthroned as King of kings presides over the dynasty that his heavenly authority legitimised.
facts: Leo VI's earlier solidi (886–908) show the Virgin orans instead of Christ; the enthroned Christ appears on this joint issue with Constantine VII.
The same Christ enthroned with a lyre-backed throne appears in the mosaic over the Imperial Gate of Hagia Sophia, where Leo VI prostrates himself before Christ (comparison).
notes: Leo VI's Virgin-orans solidus is documented by the CNG specimen 'Solidus of Leo VI.jpg' on Commons.

summary: On the obverse Christ Pantokrator sits on a throne with a curved back, blessing and holding the Gospels, within the legend 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. The reverse shows the boy emperor Constantine VII and his mother, the empress Zoe Karbonopsina, holding a patriarchal cross between them. The enthroned Christ assures the legitimacy of a child ruler under his mother's regency.
facts: Zoe Karbonopsina, fourth wife of Leo VI, served as regent for her son Constantine VII from 913 until 919, when Romanos Lekapenos seized power (Wikipedia).
The CNG catalogue dates this specimen precisely to 6 February 914.

summary: One face of the coin shows Christ nimbate and enthroned, raising his hand in blessing and holding the Gospels, within the legend 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. The other shows the crowned busts of Romanos I Lekapenos and his eldest son and co-emperor Christopher, holding a patriarchal cross between them. Usurper though he was, Romanos placed his rule visibly under the kingship of Christ.
facts: Christopher Lekapenos, eldest son of Romanos I, was co-emperor from 921 until his death in August 931, which dates this issue (Wikipedia).

summary: On the obverse a facing bust of Christ blesses and holds the Gospels; on the reverse Constantine VII, now sole senior emperor, and his son Romanos II hold a patriarchal cross between them. The serene Pantokrator of this issue, with a carefully modelled face, reflects the classicising taste of Constantine VII's court. The coin carried Christ's image throughout the empire and far beyond its borders.
facts: Constantine VII became sole ruler in 945 after the fall of the Lekapenoi and crowned his son Romanos II co-emperor; this issue belongs to their joint reign (945–959).
notes: The CNG description notes a scuff across Christ's face on this specimen.

summary: The obverse shows the bust of Christ Pantokrator in a cross-nimbus, blessing and holding a jewelled Gospel book; on the reverse the soldier-emperor Nikephoros II Phokas and the young Basil II, the legitimate heir, hold a patriarchal cross between them. Under Nikephoros the full-weight gold coin acquired its later name, histamenon. Christ's image sanctions the partnership between the victorious general and the Macedonian dynasty.
facts: Wikipedia notes that Nikephoros II introduced a lighter gold coin, the tetarteron, after which the traditional full-weight solidus came to be called the histamenon ('standard' coin).
notes: The file name refers to the Sear catalogue; the holding collection of this specimen is not stated on Commons.

summary: The obverse presents the bust of Christ Pantokrator, blessing and holding the Gospels, in a cross-nimbus. On the reverse the Virgin Mary, with the hand of God above, joins the emperor John I Tzimiskes in holding a patriarchal cross, a sign that his rule is sanctioned from heaven. Christ above, his Mother interceding: the coin is a compact statement of Byzantine political theology.
facts: This issue continues the scheme, revived after Iconoclasm, of Christ on the obverse and the ruler on the reverse, which remained the norm of Byzantine gold coinage until the end of the Empire (Wikipedia, Byzantine coinage).

links.label: Wikimedia Commons category: Coins of Ioannes I Tzimiskes

notes: John I is traditionally credited (after the chronicler Skylitzes) with introducing the anonymous folles bearing Christ's image; this attribution is not certain and is not used as a fact here.

summary: The bust of Christ, with a jewelled cross-nimbus, blesses and holds the Gospels on the obverse; on the reverse the brothers Basil II and Constantine VIII, both crowned, hold a long cross between them. Struck in the early, troubled years of Basil's long reign, the coin continues the tradition of placing the emperors beneath Christ's authority. The broad, flat flan anticipates the later, wider histamenon.
facts: Wikipedia notes that during the later reign of Basil II (976–1025) the histamenon began to be struck thinner and wider, while the lighter tetarteron became smaller and thicker.

summary: This large bronze coin bears no emperor's portrait or name: the obverse shows the bust of Christ with a cross-nimbus, blessing and holding a Gospel book, with IC XC and the name EMMANOUEL, and the reverse carries only the words 'Jesus Christ, King of Kings' in four lines. Everyday coins like this put the image and confession of Christ into the hands of ordinary people across the Byzantine world. Worn by circulation, this specimen still shows the calm face of the Lord.
facts: Wikipedia's article on Byzantine coinage explains that in the 10th century 'anonymous folles' were struck instead of coins depicting the emperor, with the bust of Christ and the inscription meaning 'Jesus Christ, Emperor of Emperors'.
Ghent University Library's catalogue reads the obverse legend as EMMANOUEL and the reverse as IhSUS XRISTUS bASILEU bASILE, and dates this Class A2 specimen to about 976–1030.

summary: The apostle Peter stands in a gold halo, holding the keys of the Kingdom and a staff topped by a cross, his weathered face turned slightly toward the viewer. Above him, in three medallions, appear Christ at the centre with the Virgin and St John at the sides. The arrangement, recalling the portraits of officials on consular diptychs, presents Peter as the servant of the Lord who presides over him from heaven.
facts: Wikipedia describes it as a sixth-century encaustic icon, one of the oldest surviving icons of St Peter; above his head is a Deesis-like row of half-figures in medallions with Christ, the Virgin and John the Evangelist.
It survived Iconoclasm because Saint Catherine's Monastery lay outside the reach of the iconoclast emperors (context of the Sinai icons).
notes: Dated 6th century by Wikipedia; the Commons file metadata gives 7th century.

summary: On the upper part of the right wing King Abgar of Edessa, enthroned and crowned, holds out the Mandylion — the cloth bearing the face of Christ — while the apostle Thaddeus appears on the left wing; below stand monastic saints. The holy face on the cloth, the 'image not made by hands', is the true focus of the scene. The panels celebrate the arrival of this relic in Constantinople in 944 and the belief that Christ himself had left his likeness to the world.
facts: Wikipedia records that the Image of Edessa was brought to Constantinople in 944, after the city was besieged by John Kourkouas and the cloth was exchanged for Muslim prisoners.
The legend held that Abgar, king of Edessa, had written to Christ asking to be healed and received in reply a cloth miraculously imprinted with his face — the Mandylion (tradition).
notes: Abgar is often said to bear the features of Emperor Constantine VII (an interpretation, not a documented fact). A public-domain detail of Abgar with the Mandylion is 'Abgarwithimageofedessa10thcentury.jpg'.

summary: The Virgin reclines on a red mattress beside the manger where the swaddled Christ Child lies, watched by the ox and the ass, while angels hover above beneath the star. The Magi approach from the right, shepherds receive the angel's message, and below Joseph sits apart while the midwives bathe the Child. Painted in hot wax on a gold ground, the icon gathers the whole Christmas story around the newborn Lord.
facts: The encaustic technique — pigments suspended in hot wax — was used for the earliest Sinai icons before Iconoclasm and was largely abandoned later in favour of egg tempera (type).
notes: Commons dates the icon to c. 6th century; this early dating could not be confirmed from a second source and a later (7th–8th century) date is possible. Image is small (382 px).

summary: The soldier-martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, wearing the gold torques of the imperial guard and holding small crosses, look out side by side with wide, calm eyes. Between their haloes a small medallion shows the bearded face of Christ, the Lord for whom they gave their lives. The icon expresses the bond between Christ and his martyrs in the intimate, luminous manner of the earliest encaustic icons.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the Khanenko Museum holds four early Byzantine encaustic icons of the 6th and 7th centuries — among them this one — which came to the museum in 1940 and have been displayed in a dedicated room since 2004.
notes: These icons are widely reported to have been brought from Sinai by the Russian bishop Porfiry Uspensky in the 19th century; not confirmed in the source read here.

summary: St John the Baptist, gaunt and long-haired, stands in his camel-hair garment and points with his right hand, the gesture of the Forerunner who announces the Lamb of God. In the upper corners two small medallions show Christ and the Virgin, toward whom John's witness is directed. Though worn, the icon keeps the spiritual intensity of the earliest Byzantine panel paintings.
facts: Wikipedia lists 'John the Baptist' (6th century) among the four early Byzantine 'Sinai' icons of the Khanenko Museum, acquired in 1940.
notes: The medallions are small and worn in the available image; their identification as Christ (left) and the Virgin (right) follows the usual description of the icon. Image is small (436 px).

summary: Although damaged and darkened, this ancient panel still shows the Virgin holding the Christ Child on her arm in the Hodegetria pose, the two faces close together and turned toward the viewer. The Child is clothed in a golden-orange garment. It has been venerated in the former pagan temple of all the gods since its consecration to the Virgin and all the martyrs.
facts: Wikipedia states that above the high altar of the Pantheon is enshrined a 7th-century Byzantine icon of the Virgin and Child, given by Emperor Phocas to Pope Boniface IV for the dedication of the building as a church on 13 May 609.
It is among the oldest Marian icons in Rome, together with the Salus Populi Romani and the Madonna della Clemenza.
notes: The image appears to show the panel after restoration, out of its altar frame.

summary: Behind silver doors in the papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum stands Rome's most revered image of Christ, a full-length enthroned Saviour now almost entirely encased in an embossed silver revetment, through which only his painted face looks out. Venerated as 'acheiropoieta', not made by human hands, it was carried in solemn procession through Rome for centuries. What the viewer sees today is the face of Christ framed by the goldsmith's work of Pope Innocent III.
facts: Wikipedia records the tradition that the icon was begun by St Luke and completed by an angel, hence its name 'acheiropoieta' ('not made by human hands').
The silver casing and doors seen in the photograph were added under Pope Innocent III (1198–1216), according to the photographer's caption.
notes: The original panel's date is uncertain (often placed in the 6th–7th century); the face currently visible has been repainted, and most of the image is hidden by the c. 1200 silver revetment.

summary: At the centre of the ringed head on the east face Christ stands as Judge, holding a cross and a flowering sceptre, a bird resting on his head; around him crowd the blessed on one side and the damned driven away by a devil on the other, while below St Michael weighs a soul. On the west face of the same cross Christ is shown crucified between the lance-bearer and sponge-bearer. Carved with more than a hundred figures, the cross is a sermon in stone on judgment and salvation.
facts: An inscription at the foot of the west face asks 'a prayer for Muiredach who had this cross made'; he is thought to be Muiredach mac Domhnaill (died 923), abbot of Monasterboice.

Wikipedia, following R. A. S. Macalister, counts 124 sculpted figures on the cross; the Last Judgment panel alone contains more than 45, and Christ wears a bird — possibly a phoenix, symbol of the Resurrection — on his head.
The cross stands about 5.5 m high and is widely regarded as the finest surviving Irish high cross; a cast is kept in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

summary: This very tall, slender cross stands beside the ruined church at Monasterboice; its west face is divided into panels of scriptural scenes, with the Crucifixion at the centre of the ringed head. Christ is shown on the cross with arms outstretched, in the tradition of the Irish high crosses that place the saving death of Christ at the very heart of the cross. Weathering has softened the carving, but the whole programme still leads the eye upward to the crucified Lord.
facts: Monasterboice has three high crosses, the North, West and South (Muiredach's) crosses; Wikipedia notes that the North and West crosses have suffered much more from weathering than Muiredach's Cross.
On Irish 'scripture' crosses the west face usually carries New Testament scenes, with the Crucifixion in the centre of the head (type).
notes: The Crucifixion is small in this full view of the cross.

summary: The west face of this magnificent cross centres on the Crucifixion, set in the ringed head, with further panels of the Passion on the shaft; on the east face Christ appears as Judge at the Last Judgment. Carved from fine sandstone, the figures are among the most accomplished of any Irish high cross. Displayed today in the visitor centre, it still conveys the monks' meditation on the whole drama of redemption.
facts: Wikipedia notes that its inscription asks for a prayer for Flann Sinna, King of Ireland, and Abbot Colmán, who commissioned it; it was carved around 900 and its panels include the Crucifixion, the Last Judgment and Christ in the Tomb.
The original was moved into the visitor centre in 1991 to protect it from the weather, and a replica stands on the original site.

summary: On the base of the tall Moone cross the Crucifixion is reduced to its essentials: a large, frontal Christ with outstretched arms and a long robe, flanked by the small figures of the lance-bearer and the sponge-bearer. The hard granite forced the sculptor into simple, almost geometric forms, which give the scene a striking, timeless power. Other panels of the cross show the Twelve Apostles and the Multiplication of the Loaves and Fishes.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the cross lay undiscovered until 1835, when two sections were found in the graveyard; the middle section was found only in 1893, revealing its full height of 17.5 feet (5.3 m), the second tallest high cross in Ireland.
Its panels include Daniel in the lions' den, the three children in the furnace and the miracle of the loaves and fishes; unusually, the scenes are concentrated on the base.
notes: Image shows the Crucifixion panel on the base, not the whole cross. The Commons file labels this the east face.

summary: Standing now inside the old church at Durrow, this high cross shows at the centre of its ringed head the crucified Christ, arms stretched along the cross-arms and surrounded by small figures. The shaft below is covered with panels of figures and interlace. Durrow, famous for its gospel book, was one of the great Columban monasteries, and its cross placed Christ's saving death before the community's eyes.
facts: Wikipedia lists among the monuments at Durrow Abbey 'a mid-ninth century high cross', and counts Durrow with Kells and Monasterboice among the sites of the 'classic' Irish high crosses.

summary: At the centre of the weathered head on the west face of this cross Christ is shown crucified, his arms outstretched along the arms of the cross, with figures pressing in from either side. The cross is dedicated by its inscription to Saints Patrick and Columba, the patrons of Irish Christianity and of the Columban monastery of Kells. Though worn, the carving still conveys the Irish devotion to Christ crucified at the heart of the monastic enclosure.
facts: It is the oldest of the five high crosses at Kells and bears an inscription naming Saints Patrick and Columba, from which it takes its alternative name (photographer's documentation).
Wikipedia notes that the round tower and high crosses at Kells are a National Monument of Ireland.
notes: The image is a weathered close view from below; the identification of the central figure as the crucified Christ follows the usual west-face scheme but the photograph is not sharp.

summary: The centre of the cross-head on the west face shows the Crucifixion, flanked on the arms by scenes from the lives of St Peter and of the desert fathers Paul and Anthony, including the Denial of Peter. Christ is set at the meeting point of the arms, the axis on which all the other stories turn. The cross once stood at the abbey's eastern gate, marking the threshold of the monastic town.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the 9th-century Market Cross originally stood at the abbey's eastern gate; legend says it was damaged by Cromwellian soldiers and used for hangings after the 1798 rebellion.
An inscription on its west face records its re-erection in 1688 (photographer's documentation).

summary: On the west face of this tall Northumbrian cross shaft, beneath a panel of John the Baptist holding the Lamb of God, Christ stands in an arched niche, his feet resting on the heads of two beasts, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a scroll. Below, a long runic inscription and the figure of a man with a falcon complete the face. The image presents Christ as Judge, recognised and acclaimed even by the creatures of the wilderness.
facts: Wikipedia notes that only the west face carries human figures; Christ is lifted on the heads of two identical creatures, as on the Ruthwell Cross, and is to be understood as 'Christ the Judge recognised by the beasts'.

The cross also bears what is 'by far the earliest English sundial to survive', and Nikolaus Pevsner called the Bewcastle and Ruthwell crosses 'the greatest achievement of their date in the whole of Europe'.
notes: Image is a 1912 black-and-white photograph (Albert S. Cook).

summary: In the upper panel of the shaft Christ sits in majesty, haloed and holding a book, flanked by angels; below, haloed busts of the apostles are stacked in arched compartments, turning toward one another as if in conversation. The faces, soft and individual, show the influence of Late Antique and Carolingian models on Northumbrian sculptors. The cross gathered the apostolic Church around its Lord.
facts: Wikipedia records that four fragments survive; three were reused in the late 12th century in rebuilding St Agatha's Church, Easby, while the fragment with Christ in Majesty was recovered from a nearby field wall before 1869 and sold to the V&A in 1931.
Unusually, the stone is not local: it matches sandstone from the Aislaby quarries near Whitby, nearly 60 miles away.
notes: Image shows the upper part of the shaft (Christ in Majesty and apostles), not the whole reconstruction.

summary: Near the foot of the east face of this slender Viking-age cross a small panel shows Christ crucified, arms outstretched, with a figure piercing his side with a lance and a woman with a long trailing dress below. The rest of the cross is covered with scenes from Norse mythology — the binding of Loki, the fight of Víðarr with the wolf — which the carver seems to have set in dialogue with the Christian story. Christ's death appears as the true victory over the powers of chaos.
facts: Wikipedia explains that the Crucifixion panel has been compared with the death of Baldr in Norse myth, the lance-bearer Longinus and Mary Magdalene paralleling figures of the pagan story, as a way of presenting Christianity to a Scandinavian audience.
The Victoria and Albert Museum had a cast of the cross made in 1882, shortly after its pagan imagery was recognised.
notes: Image is an 1883 engraving of the panel (public domain), not a photograph of the whole cross.

summary: On the front of this Lombard altar Christ sits frontally within a mandorla carried by four flying angels, holding a book and blessing, while cherubim appear beside him. The flat, linear carving and the large heads and hands of the figures are typical of Lombard sculpture. The sides show the Visitation and the Adoration of the Magi, so that the altar unites the Incarnation with the glory of Christ.
facts: The altar is dated 737–744, while Ratchis, son of Duke Pemmo, ruled Friuli before becoming king of the Lombards in 744 (Wikipedia; museum dating recorded with the photographs).
The relief was originally painted; the museum presents a multimedia reconstruction of its original colours.

summary: Set within an arched frame on the exterior wall of the church, Christ sits frontally with a cross-nimbus, blessing with his right hand and holding a book, his robe falling in stylised folds. The relief belongs to the extraordinary programme of biblical carvings that wraps around the whole church. Built as a palace church for King Gagik of Vaspurakan, the church presented Christ as Lord over the royal island and its people.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the unique importance of the church comes from the extensive array of bas-relief carvings of mostly biblical scenes that adorn its external walls.
It was built of pink volcanic tuff by the architect-monk Manuel in 915–921 as a palatine church for King Gagik I Artsruni of Vaspurakan.

links.label: Wikipedia: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar

notes: The exact position of this relief on the façade is not stated in the source read.

summary: Two crowded registers of small, round-headed figures tell the Gospel story: in the upper band Christ washes the feet of Peter and the Lamb of God is shown on a cross surrounded by the evangelist symbols, and in the lower band Christ, standing in a mandorla, is carried up to heaven by angels as the apostles watch. Further scenes fill the rest of the slab. Buried face down for centuries, the stone preserves a rare Anglo-Saxon narrative cycle of Christ's saving work.
facts: Wikipedia records that the large Anglo-Saxon coffin lid was discovered under the chancel floor near the sanctuary in 1820 and is now mounted on the north wall of the nave.
notes: Scene identifications are made from the photograph and follow common readings; individual scenes (e.g. the Ascension versus the Descent into Hell) are debated. Date estimates vary from the 7th to the early 9th century.

summary: On the left leaf a bearded Christ sits enthroned beneath a shell-headed niche, holding a jewelled book and blessing, flanked by Saints Peter and Paul; on the right leaf the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child on her lap, between two archangels. The two leaves answer each other as the heavenly King and his Mother, each attended by a celestial court. This imperial-looking pair is among the most majestic Christian ivories of the age of Justinian.
facts: Pairing Christ enthroned among apostles with the Virgin enthroned among angels on facing leaves became a model for later Byzantine icon pairs on templon screens (type).
The leaves follow the format of the official consular diptychs of the period, but replace the consul with Christ and the Virgin (type).
notes: Museum record not accessible; the attribution to Constantinople is the usual one in the literature.

summary: Around this ivory box a youthful, beardless Christ sits on a high-backed throne, teaching from an open scroll, while the apostles stand or sit around him in animated discussion, like philosophers around a master. The other side of the pyxis shows Abraham about to sacrifice Isaac, the Old Testament prefiguration of Christ's sacrifice. The classical poise of the figures makes this one of the most beautiful of all Early Christian ivories.
facts: Christ enthroned as teacher among the apostles was one of the favourite images of Christ in the late 4th and early 5th centuries, borrowed from the iconography of philosophers and their pupils (type).
The museum label describes its origin as unknown and dates it to about 400.

summary: A youthful Christ, carrying a long cross-staff, strides toward a kneeling sick man and stretches out his hand to heal him, while apostles, one holding a jewelled book, follow behind. The deep, rounded carving gives the figures strong volume around the curve of the tusk. Boxes like this probably held the Eucharistic bread or relics, so that the images of healing surrounded what they contained.
facts: The museum attributes the pyxis to Egypt in the second half of the 6th century; Alexandria was a major centre of ivory carving in Late Antiquity (context).
notes: The specific miracles are not identified in the accessible label.

summary: Three scenes are stacked on this narrow ivory leaf: at the top Herod, enthroned, orders the Massacre of the Innocents; in the middle John the Baptist lays his hand on the head of the small, naked Christ standing in the stream of the Jordan; and at the bottom the haloed Christ touches with his staff the water jars at the wedding at Cana as a servant pours. The panel moves from the threat to the infant Christ to his manifestation at the Jordan and his first sign at Cana.
facts: The museum attributes the panel to Rome or Milan in the first half of the 5th century; it probably formed part of a five-part book cover or diptych (type).
In Early Christian art Christ often performs miracles with a staff or wand, as here at Cana (type).

summary: Forty naked soldiers huddle and writhe on the frozen lake of Sebaste, where they were condemned to die of cold for their faith; one turns away toward the warm bath-house at the right. Above them Christ sits enthroned in heaven between angels holding crowns, ready to reward their endurance. The plaque is a masterpiece of Byzantine figure carving, contrasting suffering below with the calm glory of Christ above.
facts: The museum records that the plaque (inv. 574) was acquired in 1828 from the Bartoldi collection.

According to the traditional accounts, the Forty Martyrs were soldiers of the Legio XII Fulminata martyred near Sebaste in Lesser Armenia in 320; the earliest account is a homily of Basil of Caesarea (Wikipedia).

summary: The face of this pilgrim's flask shows the Virgin enthroned frontally with the Christ Child on her lap, with the star above; the Magi approach from one side bearing gifts and the shepherds with their flocks from the other. A Greek inscription runs around the rim. Brought back from the Holy Land filled with oil from the holy places, such flasks carried images of the Gospel events that had taken place there.
facts: Wikipedia describes the Monza ampullae as the largest collection of Early Medieval pilgrimage flasks for holy oil from the Holy Land, made in Palestine probably in the 5th to early 7th centuries and kept in Monza Cathedral since they were donated by Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards (c. 570–628).
They were mass-produced souvenirs, filled with oil from lamps burning before the holy shrines, and their images played a crucial part in establishing the iconography of many Christian subjects.
notes: The only freely licensed image found is a historic glass lantern slide (University of Leuven) reproducing an engraving of the ampulla, not a photograph of the object. The specific ampulla number in Monza could not be identified.

summary: An ivory plaque of the Crucifixion is set in a jewelled silver frame: Christ hangs on the cross, with the Virgin and St John below and busts of the sun and moon in medallions above. Gems of red, green and blue alternate with discs of filigree around the border. Used as a 'pax', it was passed among the faithful to be kissed during Mass, so that the image of the crucified Lord became an instrument of peace.
facts: A pax (or osculatory) was a tablet offered to the clergy and congregation to kiss at the sign of peace during Mass (liturgical use).
It is traditionally associated with a Duke Ursus (Orso) of Friuli, from whom it takes its name; the museum dates it to the mid-9th century.
notes: The association with Duke Ursus is traditional. Some captions date it 850–900.

summary: On the cup of this great chalice an oval medallion shows Christ in half-length, blessing and holding a book, flanked by the letters alpha and omega and the initials of 'Iesus Salvator'; four further medallions show the evangelists with their symbols. Interlace and animal ornament cover the rest of the vessel. Raised at the altar, the chalice placed the image of Christ the Saviour directly above the wine of the Eucharist.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the chalice was donated by Liutperga, wife of the Bavarian duke Tassilo III, possibly when Kremsmünster Abbey was founded in 777; the inscription round the foot reads TASSILO DUX FORTIS + LIVTPIRG VIRGA REGALIS.
It stands 25.5 cm high and holds about 1.75 litres; although synods forbade copper and bronze for consecrated chalices, it is one of the few surviving examples of such vessels.
notes: Photographed while on loan to the exhibition 'Charlemagne – Power, Art, Treasures' at the Centre Charlemagne, Aachen.
